transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 11:00 AM PT / 2:00 PM ET
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Riverbank Head of ML), Priya Shah (Riverbank CTO), Marta Reyes (Riverbank SRE)

Summary (auto-gen - may be rough): Quick hosted API demo focused on chat and text generation basics. Covered streaming responses, key params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), retry behavior and idempotency, basic rate limiting and cost/latency tradeoffs. Discussed security questions (SOC2, SSO) and next steps for POC benchmarks.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jordan from Redwood, I'm the AE, with me is Samira, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Liam: Good, thanks. Sorry for the slight delay, we were wrapping up another sync.
[00:09] Priya: All good here. Looking forward to the demo.
[00:12] Samira: Awesome, I'll share my screen in a sec. Today we'll walk through hosted API for chat and text generation—mainly streaming, the common params you tweak, and how retries work. We'll also touch on observability in the Console and a few Optimize tips.
[00:25] Jordan: Quick intro—Riverbank, you mentioned fraud detection and customer support auto-responses as two high-level use cases, is that still right?
[00:30] Liam: Yep, exactly. And we have a nightly batch job that generates account summaries, so latency is less critical there but cost is. For some real-time chat features latency matters.
[00:39] Marta: And our infra constraint is that any PII must not leave our VPC for the pilot; we want to understand how hosted fits with that.
[00:46] Samira: Great to note. We'll go over retention, encryption, and what Private would look like vs Hosted. Quick clarification: hosted API can be used with customer-managed keys for encryption at rest?
[00:56] Jordan: Short answer: yes, for Private we integrate KMS/HSM. For hosted we have SOC2 controls and customer data retention options—I'll attach the security pack after.
[01:06] Samira: Ok I'm sharing my screen — starting with a simple chat request. (screen) Here's a standard curl example to /v1/chat/completions. Notice the streaming flag, we set streaming: true.
[01:20] Samira: When streaming, the server sends partial deltas back as tokens are generated, so your UI can render progressively. This reduces perceived latency.
[01:28] Priya: How do you handle ordering or partial failures in streaming? If a connection drops do we re-request and re-play?
[01:34] Samira: Good q. Our client libraries provide an offset cursor and message id. If a connection drops you can resume from last acknowledged token where supported; otherwise typical pattern is to re-issue with the same conversation id and rely on idempotency keys to avoid double side-effects. Retries are capped and exponential backoff by default.
[01:50] Liam: You mentioned params earlier—what's the interplay between temperature, top_p and deterministic outputs for fraud rules?
[01:56] Samira: For deterministic behavior, keep temperature near 0 and top_p low. For reranking or creative summaries you might use higher temp. For fraud rules we usually recommend deterministic profiles or a small ensemble with reranker.
[02:08] Jordan: Also cost wise, you can limit max_tokens and use streaming to stop early if thresholds met.
[02:14] Marta: On retries—how do you guarantee not to double-bill tokens if a retry happens mid-stream?
[02:20] Samira: We have request ids and, for hosted API, token counting is tied to the final accepted response. If a retry is a duplicate due to network flake we try to dedupe on our end; but best practice is client-side idempotency keys.
[02:31] Priya: Any rate limits? We're going to hit spikes up to 400 qps in certain windows.
[02:36] Jordan: Hosted has tiered limits; for higher sustained qps we suggest Dedicated/reserved capacity. We can also do burst policies. For the demo I can show how to see per-route throughput in Console.
[02:47] Samira: Switching to Console briefly — here's the per-model dashboard, token consumption, latencies, and trace links. You can set alerts on regressions or quality metrics.
[02:56] Liam: Nice, can we see token breakdown by customer route?
[03:00] Samira: Yes, per-route and per-api-key breakdowns. That helps with cost attribution.
[03:06] Jordan: Back to code — here's a small Node snippet showing retry policy: maxRetries=3, backoffFactor=2, and a jitter. We recommend clients implement exponential backoff to avoid thundering herds.
[03:18] Liam: For POC we'll probably simulate our payloads — we'll share some sample prompt templates.
[03:21] Samira: Perfect. One thing to note—KV cache/prefix caching can save tokens if you have repeated context. For summaries where the prefix is common you can get big savings.
[03:31] Priya: You said KV cache, can you expand? I think our infra lead misheard earlier: is that the K V cache like in Redis?
[03:36] Samira: It's internal to the runtime—key/value cache for past key/value attention states, not a separate Redis, but it works with our batching to reduce repeated compute. I'll drop a short note in the follow-up.
[03:46] Marta: Security quick: SSO, RBAC and audit logs — we need SAML and ability to get audit trails for tokens.
[03:52] Jordan: We're SOC2 and have SSO with SAML/SCIM, RBAC in console, and comprehensive audit logs. I'll include our SOC2 cert page and the SAML guide.
[04:01] Liam: Any compliance for EU data residency? We have EU customers.
[04:05] Jordan: We support region pinning and data residency options; for strict controls we can look at Private deployments.
[04:11] Priya: Cost question—how do you benchmark cost per 1k responses? We need a ballpark for planning.
[04:16] Samira: It's model-dependent and sequence-length dependent. For planning use our cost estimator in Console; for the POC we'll run representative samples and give you per-1k numbers.
[04:25] Jordan: Ok quick demo of streaming behavior — I'll trigger a sample prompt and show partial tokens. (short pause) You can see chunks arrive, and in the client we append.
[04:40] Liam: Looks smooth. If we wanted to fall back to a smaller model on high load, is that automatic?
[04:45] Samira: We have smart routing policies. You can define fallback to cheaper compatible variants when latency or capacity thresholds are hit. Automatic fallback is configurable.
[04:54] Priya: Great. Any limits on model switching wrt context compatibility?
[04:58] Samira: Models need to be architecture-compatible; some runtime features like fancy kv cache are model-specific, so tests are recommended.
[05:05] Jordan: Alright, recap — next steps: Jordan will send pricing and security pack; Samira will run sample bench and share; Riverbank sends sample prompts and peak qps windows. We'll aim to kick off POC mid-March.
[05:18] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks, this was helpful.
[05:21] Liam: Thanks all.
[05:23] Marta: Thanks.

(End of call)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings (K V cache spelled out by the transcriber, 'Red wood' or 'Redwood Dedicated' variations), filler words and small interruptions left as-is. Links/attachments referenced: "Security pack (SOC2, SAML guide)", "Pricing sheet (linked)", "Sample bench results (to be added)".
